subject: Private runtime: firewall stewardship & ephemeral egress authorization
messages:
From: Jack Curtis <jack.curtis@medicorps.com>
To: Dylan Brooks <dylan@redwood.ai>
Cc: Medicorps Procurement <procurement@medicorps.com>
Date: 2025-09-30T08:12:00-07:00
Subject: Private runtime egress: allowlist and ephemeral IPs

Hi Dylan —

Thanks for the call earlier. As we spin up the private deployment (VPC) for Medicorps we need a clear list of what the perimeter team will need to approve from a firewall/allowlist standpoint. A few specifics from our side:

- We prefer not to maintain long-lived static IP reservations for each tenant; can Redwood support a short-lived NAT pool with documented ownership and rotation?
- We need a certifiable evidence packet for our auditors (SOC2) that shows outbound destinations, FQDNs, and the signed attestation that Redwood control plane calls originate from a small number of managed IPs.
- Is there a recommended fallback behavior if our perimeter blocks SNI inspection (we currently TLS pass-through to avoid rewriting)?

Attaching a network diagram in the next email. Can you confirm what minimal firewall rules we should open (ports, IPs/FQDNs), and which of those are acceptable to express as FQDN instead of fixed IPs? Also: any operational windows needed for IP rotation?

Appreciate the quick turnaround — procurement wants the evidence pack for approval.

—Jack
Senior Cloud Ops, Medicorps
From: Dylan Brooks <dylan@redwood.ai>
To: Jack Curtis <jack.curtis@medicorps.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>, Laura Bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.ai>
Date: 2025-09-30T09:20:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Private runtime egress: allowlist and ephemeral IPs

Jack — thanks for the clear ask and the call. Quick summary of what we can offer and the decision points for your perimeter team: 

1) Static vs ephemeral egress
- We support three patterns: (A) static, customer-allocated public IPs (long-lived) behind NAT; (B) a small, short-lived NAT pool we operate with documented rotation and ownership; (C) per-tenant outbound via a customer-managed proxy (your side) so egress appears from your IPs.
- For auditor friendliness, pattern B (ephemeral pool) plus an evidence pack is common: we provide rotation schedule, signed manifest of IPs used per-day, and per-request metadata in logs.

2) FQDN vs IP allowlisting
- FQDN allowlisting is possible for control-plane endpoints and certain telemetry endpoints, but note that some firewalls (esp. FQDN-based rules) rely on DNS TTLs — we publish expected FQDNs and CNAMEs and recommend also allowing the hosted provider IP ranges as a fallback when DNS resolution is unreliable.

3) TLS passthrough (SNI) and inspection
- If you plan to keep TLS passthrough for inbound tenant traffic, that does not affect Redwood egress. For our control plane and runtime outbound requests, SNI-inspection or mTLS to our managed proxies can be supported. If you cannot do SNI inspection, we recommend:
  - Use mTLS from the runtime to the Redwood control plane/proxy (we can provide client certs) OR
  - Allow a short list of outbound FQDNs and enable TLS SNI inspection for those flows.

4) Ports and minimal rules
- Outbound: 443 (https) to our control-plane and blob stores; 853/53 if you perform DNS over TLS; optional 80 for ACME/challenges.
- Inbound: depends on VPC peering / transit config — we'll provide an example ACL file.

5) Rotation windows
- For ephemeral NAT pools we rotate on a daily or weekly cadence. If you need a stable IP for SLA or firewall reasons during cutover, we can carve a reserved window (e.g., 48–72h) then shift to rotation. Communication happens 48h in advance by default.

Next steps — I'll get Ben to outline the evidence pack requirements and Laura will propose the minimal ACL snippet your perimeter can share with auditors.

—Dylan
Director, Solution Architecture
Redwood Inference
From: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>
To: Dylan Brooks <dylan@redwood.ai>, Jack Curtis <jack.curtis@medicorps.com>
Cc: Laura Bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.ai>, Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie_nguyen@redwood.ai>
Date: 2025-10-01T10:05:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Private runtime egress: allowlist and ephemeral IPs

Following up with the evidence pack outline for SOC2 / perimeter teams. Jack — what your auditors typically ask for is in two buckets: operational evidence and cryptographic proof. Our standard deliverables (we can customize) are: 

Operational evidence:
- Daily NAT manifest (CSV): timestamp, egress_ip, instance_id, model_variant, justification tag.
- Aggregated egress histogram (by FQDN) for the audit window.
- Network topology diagram with annotated egress paths (we can co-brand with your diagram).

Cryptographic / attestation items:
- Signed manifest (PGP-signed or PKCS7) showing the IP set in-scope for the audit period.
- TLS client certs and fingerprint manifest for mTLS-enabled flows.
- Hash of log bundle + signature so auditors can verify integrity.

Notes on technical constraints:
- If you require per-tenant fixed IPs we can allocate but it is operationally heavy (N IPs per tenant). We strongly prefer small NAT pools and high-fidelity logs.
- FQDN-only rules are acceptable for control-plane endpoints, but for data-plane blobs (e.g., model downloads) we recommend IP allowlisting or a proxy because CDNs often change A records.

I'll prepare a template evidence bundle (sample files + README) and attach as a zip once we have your audit window.

—Ben
Security & Compliance, Redwood Inference
From: Laura Bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.ai>
To: Jack Curtis <jack.curtis@medicorps.com>, Dylan Brooks <dylan@redwood.ai>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>
Date: 2025-10-01T15:30:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Private runtime egress: allowlist and ephemeral IPs

Jack — operational checklist below (minimal ACL snippet + questions):

Minimal outbound ACL (example)
- Allow TCP 443 to: runtime-control.redwood-inference.com, telemetry.redwood-inference.com, artifacts.redwood-inference-cdn.net
- Allow UDP/53 and TCP/853 to your resolver(s) if you use DNS over TLS
- Optionally allow TCP 22 from our ops jump hosts for troubleshooting (restricted by src IP; requires prior approval)

Questions for your network team
- Do you accept FQDN-based rules that resolve via your internal resolver, or must we provide IP blocks?
- Is there an existing maintenance window for NAT pool rotations or can we negotiate a carve-out?
- Who is the canonical contact for emergency IP remediation (name/email)?

Operational notes
- We'll provide a terraform-friendly ACL snippet and a one-page operational runbook for your network team.
- For SNI-inspection limitations: we can provide client certs and a short-lived mTLS credential to the runtime; this is the recommended path if you want to avoid allowing broad IP ranges.

If you can answer the three questions above we can deliver the template evidence bundle by EOD Friday.

—Laura
Principal PM, Operations
Redwood Inference
From: Jack Curtis <jack.curtis@medicorps.com>
To: Dylan Brooks <dylan@redwood.ai>
Cc: Medicorps Procurement <procurement@medicorps.com>, Laura Bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.ai>, Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>
Date: 2025-10-02T16:45:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Private runtime egress: allowlist and ephemeral IPs

Thanks — this is exactly what we needed. Answers below and attachments included.

Answers:
- We prefer FQDN-based rules for control plane endpoints, but will require IP allowlisting for artifact downloads (CDN). We will run DNS resolution tests to confirm TTL behavior.
- Maintenance window: we have a rolling Q2 maintenance window that can be used for rotation hand-offs. For the first two weeks of production we can accept a 72h pinned window for cutover.
- Emergency contact: me (jack.curtis@medicorps.com) and our on-call netops lead: Priya Shah <priya.shah@medicorps.com>.

Attachments: medicorps_network_diagram.pdf (network diagram), egress-evidence.zip (sample audit checklist template we use).

Next steps requested from Redwood:
1) Provide the terraform ACL snippet + one-page runbook.
2) Sample evidence bundle (Ben) with a signed manifest for a 30-day window.
3) mTLS client certs option and instructions (if we choose that path).

We are OK with the ephemeral NAT pool model (pattern B) provided we get the signed manifests and rotation schedule for the first 30 days. Procurement will attach those to the contract.

—Jack
Senior Cloud Ops, Medicorps
